segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and marvelous: seven angels with seven plagues, the last ones, because with them the fury of God is completed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw what looked like a sea of glass mixed with fire, and those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing on the sea of glass, holding harps of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they sing the song of Moses, the slave of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Great and marvelous are your works, Lord God, the Almighty! Righteous and true are your ways, King of the ages!

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Who will not fear you, Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. For all the nations will come and worship before you, for your righteous acts have been revealed.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After these things I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of testimony in heaven was opened,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the seven angels who had the seven plagues came out of the sanctuary, clothed in clean, bright linen and with golden sashes wrapped around their chests.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the fury of God, who lives forever and ever.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.

notes.note: Revelation uses two Greek words for God’s anger, sometimes side by side (16:19; 19:15), and most English versions render both as “wrath.” The word here is the more passionate of the two, used in the period for an outburst of anger. “Fury” keeps it distinct from the other word, which is rendered “wrath.”

The verb is the ordinary Greek word for winning a battle or a contest, and “conquer” keeps that note of victory better than “overcome.” The construction is unusual: literally “those conquering out of the beast,” probably meaning those who came out of the struggle with the beast as victors. The meaning is not disputed, and several modern versions also use “conquer” in Revelation.

notes.phrase: standing on the sea of glass
notes.traditional: standing beside the sea of glass
notes.note: The preposition can mean either “on” or “at, beside.” Many modern versions choose “beside,” which strengthens the echo of Israel standing on the shore of the sea in Exodus 14–15. “On” is the more usual sense of the construction in Revelation and suits a sea that is like a glass pavement before God’s throne (4:6).

The Greek word is the ordinary one for a slave, a person owned by a master, and that is what a first-century reader heard. Most English versions have “servant,” echoing the Old Testament title of honor “Moses the servant of the LORD.” The point of the title is that Moses belonged wholly to God and acted on his authority.

The scene recalls Exodus 15, where Moses and Israel sing beside the sea after their rescue from Pharaoh. Deuteronomy 32 is also called a song of Moses. The words that follow are not a quotation of either song but a weaving together of Old Testament phrases, especially from the Psalms, Deuteronomy 32:4, and Jeremiah 10:7.

The manuscripts are divided between “King of the ages” and “King of the nations,” and both readings have early support. The Greek text translated here reads “ages”; other critical editions and many modern versions prefer “nations,” which fits the allusion to Jeremiah 10:7. The King James Version’s “King of saints” rests on very slight evidence.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. Many versions have “Just and true are your ways” here. “Righteous” is used so that the link with “your righteous acts” in verse 4, a word from the same family, can be heard; that word could also be understood as God’s just judgments.

Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the building where God dwells. This translation renders the second as “sanctuary” throughout. Most versions have “temple” here.

The word traditionally rendered “tabernacle” is the ordinary Greek word for a tent. “Tent of testimony” is the Greek Old Testament’s name for Israel’s portable wilderness sanctuary, which housed the tablets of the covenant, called “the testimony.” The phrase probably means “the sanctuary, that is, the tent of testimony”: John sees the heavenly original of that tent.

A few important early manuscripts read “stone” instead of “linen”; the two Greek words differ by a single letter. Most editors regard “stone” as a copying slip, though a few have defended it as the harder reading in light of Ezekiel 28:13.

In the Old Testament, cloud or smoke filling the sanctuary marks the overwhelming presence of God. Moses could not enter the tent when the cloud of glory filled it (Exodus 40:34–35), and the priests could not stand to minister at the dedication of Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 8:10–11). See also Isaiah 6:4.

candidates.reason: It must be kept distinct from ὀργή (“wrath”) across Revelation, especially where the two are combined in 16:19 and 19:15, and translators vary between wrath, fury, anger and passion.
Slave versus servant affects well over a hundred verses, including honorific titles such as “slave of God” for Moses, the prophets and the apostles, and needs one policy.
It is a different word from ἅγιος and is rendered variously as holy, devout or faithful (Acts 2:27; 13:35; Heb 7:26; Rev 16:5); a decision is needed on whether to distinguish it.
The instrument is strictly a lyre; “harp” is traditional, and the choice should match across Revelation 5:8, 14:2, 15:2 and 1 Corinthians 14:7.
It recurs nine times in Revelation and in 2 Corinthians 6:18; translators vary between “Almighty,” “the Almighty” and “All-Powerful,” and the divine title should be uniform.
